claim: Abiraterone acetate is an effective treatment for metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC).
source: Abiraterone acetate is an effective treatment for metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but evolution of resistance inevitably leads to progression.
evidence: This is stated as established background in the abstract without specific data from this study, drawing on general medical knowledge.

claim: Evolution of resistance to abiraterone inevitably leads to progression in mCRPC.
source: Abiraterone acetate is an effective treatment for metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but evolution of resistance inevitably leads to progression.
evidence: This is stated as established background knowledge about treatment resistance.

claim: 17 subjects were enrolled in the adaptive therapy group.
source: 17 subjects were enrolled in the adaptive therapy group and 16 in the SOC group.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study cohort size, representing data from the trial.

claim: 16 subjects were enrolled in the SOC (standard of care) group.
source: 17 subjects were enrolled in the adaptive therapy group and 16 in the SOC group.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the control cohort size, representing data from the trial.

claim: All SOC subjects have progressed.
source: All SOC subjects have progressed, but four patients in the study cohort remain stably cycling (range 53–70 months).
evidence: This is an observational outcome from the trial data.

claim: Four patients in the adaptive therapy cohort remain stably cycling with a range of 53–70 months.
source: All SOC subjects have progressed, but four patients in the study cohort remain stably cycling (range 53–70 months).
evidence: This is an observational outcome from the trial data showing duration of response.

claim: The adaptive therapy cohort had a median time to progression of 33.5 months.
source: The study cohort had significantly improved median time to progression (TTP; 33.5 months; p<0.001)
evidence: This is a measured outcome from the trial data.

claim: The adaptive therapy cohort had significantly improved median time to progression compared to the SOC cohort (p<0.001).
source: The study cohort had significantly improved median time to progression (TTP; 33.5 months; p<0.001) and median overall survival (OS; 58.5 months; hazard ratio, 0.41, 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.20–0.83, p<0.001) compared to 14.3 and 31.3 months in the SOC cohort.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of trial outcomes with p-value provided.

claim: The adaptive therapy cohort had a median overall survival of 58.5 months.
source: The study cohort had significantly improved median time to progression (TTP; 33.5 months; p<0.001) and median overall survival (OS; 58.5 months; hazard ratio, 0.41, 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.20–0.83, p<0.001) compared to 14.3 and 31.3 months in the SOC cohort.
evidence: This is a measured outcome from the trial data.

claim: The adaptive therapy cohort had significantly improved median overall survival compared to the SOC cohort with a hazard ratio of 0.41 (95% CI, 0.20–0.83, p<0.001).
source: The study cohort had significantly improved median time to progression (TTP; 33.5 months; p<0.001) and median overall survival (OS; 58.5 months; hazard ratio, 0.41, 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.20–0.83, p<0.001) compared to 14.3 and 31.3 months in the SOC cohort.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of trial outcomes with hazard ratio and confidence interval provided.

claim: The SOC cohort had a median time to progression of 14.3 months.
source: The study cohort had significantly improved median time to progression (TTP; 33.5 months; p<0.001) and median overall survival (OS; 58.5 months; hazard ratio, 0.41, 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.20–0.83, p<0.001) compared to 14.3 and 31.3 months in the SOC cohort.
evidence: This is a measured outcome from the control cohort data.

claim: The SOC cohort had a median overall survival of 31.3 months.
source: The study cohort had significantly improved median time to progression (TTP; 33.5 months; p<0.001) and median overall survival (OS; 58.5 months; hazard ratio, 0.41, 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.20–0.83, p<0.001) compared to 14.3 and 31.3 months in the SOC cohort.
evidence: This is a measured outcome from the control cohort data.

claim: Study subjects received no abiraterone during 46% of time on trial on average.
source: On average, study subjects received no abiraterone during 46% of time on trial.
evidence: This is a calculated metric from the trial data showing treatment-free intervals.

claim: The competition coefficient ratio (αRS/αSR) of sensitive and resistant populations was two- to threefold higher than pre-trial estimates.
source: Longitudinal trial data demonstrated the competition coefficient ratio (αRS/αSR) of sensitive and resistant populations, a critical factor in intratumoral evolution, was two- to threefold higher than pre-trial estimates.
evidence: This is derived from mathematical modeling analysis of longitudinal trial data.

claim: Computer simulations in the four long-term survivors found that cycled therapy significantly decreased the resistant population due to the larger value for αRS/αSR.
source: Computer simulations of intratumoral evolutionary dynamics in the four long-term survivors found that, due to the larger value for αRS/αSR, cycled therapy significantly decreased the resistant population.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling using updated parameters from trial data.

claim: Simulations in subjects who progressed predicted further increases in OS could be achieved with prompt abiraterone withdrawal after achieving 50% PSA reduction.
source: Simulations in subjects who progressed predicted further increases in OS could be achieved with prompt abiraterone withdrawal after achieving 50% PSA reduction.
evidence: This is a prediction from computational modeling based on trial data analysis.

claim: Nearly all cancer treatments ultimately fail due to evolution of resistance.
source: While often initially effective, nearly all cancer treatments ultimately fail due to evolution of resistance (Sarmento-Ribeiro et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Prior efforts to disrupt the molecular machinery of resistance (such as P-glycoprotein during chemotherapy administration) have led to small or no improvement in outcomes.
source: Prior efforts to disrupt the molecular machinery of resistance (such as P-glycoprotein during chemotherapy administration) have led to small or no improvement in outcomes (Vasan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tumor cells generally have multiple available mechanisms of resistance.
source: Prior efforts to disrupt the molecular machinery of resistance (such as P-glycoprotein during chemotherapy administration) have led to small or no improvement in outcomes (Vasan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019), indicating that tumor cells generally have multiple available mechanisms of resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure of single-mechanism resistance inhibition strategies, supported by citations.

claim: Resistant tumors require both deployment of molecular mechanisms of resistance and proliferation of surviving resistant populations to become clinically significant.
source: However, resistant tumors, regardless of the precise mechanism, require both deployment of molecular mechanisms of resistance and proliferation of surviving (i.e., resistant) populations to become clinically significant (Gatenby et al., 2009a; Reed et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Current treatment strategies that apply therapy at maximum tolerated dose until progression are often not evolutionarily optimal.
source: Evolution-based models show that current treatment strategies, which apply therapy at maximum tolerated dose until progression, are often not evolutionarily optimal.
evidence: This is based on predictions from evolution-based mathematical models.

claim: Maximum tolerated dose therapy strongly selects for resistance while eradicating all treatment-sensitive cells.
source: While an initial response may be large, therapy fails because it strongly selects for resistance while eradicating all treatment-sensitive cells.
evidence: This is an inference from evolutionary principles applied to cancer treatment.

claim: Resistant cells experience competitive release when treatment-sensitive cells are eradicated, allowing for rapid proliferation.
source: The resistant cells are now free from competition with sensitive cells – an evolutionary dynamic termed 'competitive release' - which allows for rapid proliferation (Silva et al., 2012; Newton and Ma, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on competitive release dynamics.

claim: Adaptive therapy exploits the fitness costs incurred by production, maintenance, and operation of the molecular machinery required for treatment resistance.
source: One evolutionary strategy to delay population growth of the resistant phenotype, termed 'adaptive therapy' (Gatenby et al., 2009b), exploits the fitness costs incurred by production, maintenance, and operation of the molecular machinery required for treatment resistance (Szakács et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on adaptive therapy and resistance costs.

claim: In the absence of treatment, the phenotypic costs of resistance reduce fitness compared to competing-sensitive cells, particularly in resource-limited tumor microenvironments.
source: However, in the absence of treatment, the phenotypic costs reduce fitness compared to competing-sensitive cells (Szakács et al., 2014), particularly in resource-limited tumor microenvironments.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents an application of evolutionary principles.

claim: When multiple mechanisms of resistance are available, the precise cost will likely vary but seldom will there be no associated cost.
source: Thus, when multiple mechanisms of resistance are available, the precise cost will likely vary but seldom will there be no associated cost.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary principles and the general nature of biological trade-offs.

claim: Population dynamics dependent on the cost of resistance are fundamental principles in pest management.
source: Population dynamics dependent on the cost of resistance are now fundamental principles in pest management (Ehler, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to pest management literature.

claim: Population dynamics dependent on the cost of resistance have been observed experimentally in cancer populations.
source: Population dynamics dependent on the cost of resistance are now fundamental principles in pest management (Ehler, 2006) and have been observed experimentally in cancer populations (Enriquez-Navas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental cancer research.

claim: There are no data regarding the molecular dynamics leading to abiraterone resistance in metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer.
source: However, there are no data regarding the molecular dynamics leading to abiraterone resistance in metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC).
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of data in the literature.

claim: The precise mechanism of abiraterone resistance may vary.
source: Furthermore, the precise mechanism of resistance may vary (Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Census methods developed in ecology can estimate relative fitness based on population distributions when direct measurements cannot be obtained.
source: When such measurements cannot be obtained, census methods developed in ecology (Pfister, 1995) can estimate relative fitness based on population distributions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to ecological methodology.

claim: If abiraterone-sensitive cells are the dominant tumor subpopulation prior to treatment, they must be fitter than the resistant phenotypes in the absence of treatment.
source: That is, if abiraterone-sensitive cells are the dominant tumor subpopulation prior to treatment, they must be fitter than the resistant phenotypes in the absence of treatment even if the specific reason for this fitness difference is not known.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological census methods and evolutionary principles.

claim: Adaptive therapy limits application of treatment to produce a moderate decrease in tumor volume while explicitly retaining a significant population of treatment-sensitive cancer cells.
source: Adaptive therapy (Gatenby et al., 2009b; Zhang et al., 2017) limits application of treatment to produce a moderate decrease in tumor volume while explicitly retaining a significant population of treatment-sensitive cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the adaptive therapy approach.

claim: In adaptive therapy, when treatment is withdrawn after initial response, sensitive cells have a fitness advantage and will proliferate at the expense of resistant cells.
source: Following an initial response, treatment is withdrawn, allowing the cancer populations to proliferate. But, in the absence of selection pressures from treatment, the sensitive cells have a fitness advantage and will proliferate at the expense of the resistant cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary principles underlying adaptive therapy.

claim: When the tumor returns to its pretreatment volume in adaptive therapy, the subpopulation distribution is similar, allowing the initial therapy to remain effective.
source: Thus, when the tumor returns to its pretreatment volume, the subpopulation distribution is similar, allowing the initial therapy to remain effective.
evidence: This is an inference based on the theoretical framework of adaptive therapy.

claim: Intermittent therapy trials in metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer randomized men into continuous or intermittent androgen deprivation therapy treatment using GnRH analogs, and neither regimen proved superior.
source: Because adaptive therapy starts and stops treatment, it is conceptually similar to 'intermittent therapy' trials in which men with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) were randomized into continuous or intermittent androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) treatment using gonadatropin releasing hormone (GnRH) analogs. Neither regimen proved superior (Hussain et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a prior clinical trial.

claim: In the intermittent therapy trial, treatment cycling began only after 8 months of induction therapy with ADT.
source: However, in the intermittent therapy trial, treatment cycling began only after 8 months of 'induction therapy' with ADT.
evidence: This is a description of the design of a prior clinical trial.

claim: In the intermittent therapy trial, intermittent dosing was permitted only if the PSA reached <4 ng/ml.
source: Furthermore, intermittent dosing was permitted only if the PSA reached <4 ng/ml.
evidence: This is a description of the design of a prior clinical trial.

claim: Computer simulations demonstrated that the prolonged induction period in the intermittent therapy trial consistently reduced the sensitive population to near-extinction levels.
source: With computer simulations (Cunningham, 2019; Cunningham et al., 2018), we have demonstrated that the prolonged induction period consistently reduced the sensitive population to near-extinction levels, as confirmed by the reduction of PSA to the normal range.
evidence: This is based on computer simulations with citations to the simulation work.

claim: The prolonged induction therapy in the intermittent therapy trial rendered adaptive therapy evolutionary dynamics impossible.
source: Since adaptive therapy relies on the presence of a sensitive cell that is initially larger than the resistant cells, the induction therapy rendered these evolutionary dynamics impossible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the principles of adaptive therapy and simulation results.

claim: Computer simulations predicted that the intermittent therapy strategy would produce tumor control identical to standard continuous full dose of ADT.
source: Thus, computer simulations predicted that this strategy would produce tumor control identical to standard continuous full dose of ADT, which was the observed outcomes with the intermittent arm indistinguishable from continuous therapy.
evidence: This is based on computer simulations that matched observed clinical trial outcomes.

claim: A prior study used intermittent ADT with fixed 8-month intervals, and model simulations showed that the intervals were too long and promoted the dominance of resistant cancer cells.
source: Similar limitations apply to a prior study that used intermittent ADT with fixed 8-month intervals (Crook et al., 2012). Model simulations showed that the intervals were too long and promoted the dominance of resistant cancer cells.
evidence: This is based on model simulations of a prior clinical trial design, supported by citation.

claim: Cancers frequently exhibit nonlinear dynamics that cannot be predicted intuitively but can be captured using mathematical models.
source: As complex adaptive systems (Uthamacumaran, 2021), cancers frequently exhibit nonlinear dynamics that cannot be predicted intuitively but can be captured using mathematical models.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents knowledge about complex systems.

claim: Computer simulations of the model were used to predict optimal trial design.
source: Computer simulations of the model were used to predict optimal trial design.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in designing the trial.

claim: The trial was a single-institution investigator-initiated pilot study (NCT02415621) carried out at the Moffitt Cancer Center, Tampa, FL.
source: This is a single-institution investigator-initiated pilot study (NCT02415621) carried out at the Moffitt Cancer Center, Tampa, FL.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the trial design and location.

claim: The protocol was approved by central IRB and monitored by Moffitt Cancer Center's protocol monitoring committee.
source: The protocol was approved by central IRB and monitored by Moffitt Cancer Center's protocol monitoring committee.
evidence: This is a statement about regulatory approval and oversight.

claim: Inclusion criteria were similar to phase III AA-302 trial population, except allowing ECOG 2 performance status, prior exposure to enzalutamide, sipuleucel-T, and ketoconazole.
source: Briefly, inclusion criteria were similar to phase III AA-302 trial (Cunningham, 2019) population, except allowing ECOG 2 performance status (PFD), prior exposure to enzalutamide, sipuleucel-T, and ketoconazole.
evidence: This describes the trial eligibility criteria with reference to a prior trial.

claim: Prior docetaxel was allowed if it was given during the castration-sensitive phase.
source: Prior docetaxel was allowed if it was given during the castration-sensitive phase.
evidence: This describes the trial eligibility criteria.

claim: Patients on opioids for cancer-related pain were excluded.
source: Patients on opioids for cancer-related pain were excluded.
evidence: This describes the trial exclusion criteria.

claim: Patients could be enrolled in the study after achieving 50% or more decline of their pre-abiraterone PSA levels.
source: Patients could be enrolled in the study after achieving 50% or more decline of their pre-abiraterone Prostate Specific Antigen (PSA) levels.
evidence: This describes the trial enrollment criteria.

claim: Cohort size was designed to have sufficient statistical power to detect a 50% increase in TTP.
source: Cohort size was designed to have sufficient statistical power to detect a 50% increase in TTP.
evidence: This describes the statistical design of the trial.

claim: Each enrolled patient began on abiraterone (1000 mg by mouth daily) and prednisone (5 mg by mouth twice daily) until achieving a >50% decline in their baseline levels of PSA pre-abiraterone.
source: Each enrolled patient began on abiraterone (1000 mg by mouth daily) and prednisone (5 mg by mouth twice daily) until achieving a >50% decline in their baseline levels of PSA pre-abiraterone.
evidence: This describes the treatment protocol.

claim: Upon achieving >50% PSA decline, abiraterone therapy was suspended.
source: Upon achieving this decline, abiraterone therapy was suspended.
evidence: This describes the treatment protocol.

claim: Tumor regression or stability was confirmed by radiographic measurements.
source: Tumor regression or stability was confirmed by radiographic measurements.
evidence: This describes the monitoring protocol.

claim: Patients were monitored every 4–6 weeks with lab tests and clinic visits.
source: Patients were monitored every 4–6 weeks with a lab (Complete Blood Count (CBC), Comprehensive Metabilic Panel (COMP), Lactic Dehydrogenase (LDH), and PSA) and clinic visit.
evidence: This describes the monitoring protocol.

claim: Every 12 weeks, each patient received a bone scan, and a computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis.
source: Every 12 weeks, each patient received a bone scan, and a computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis.
evidence: This describes the imaging protocol.

claim: Abiraterone plus prednisone were reinitiated when a patient's PSA increased to or above the pre-abiraterone PSA baseline.
source: Abiraterone plus prednisone were reinitiated when a patient's PSA increased to or above the pre-abiraterone PSA baseline.
evidence: This describes the treatment protocol for restarting therapy.

claim: Abiraterone therapy was stopped again after the patient's PSA declined to >50% of his baseline PSA.
source: Abiraterone therapy was stopped again after the patient's PSA declined to >50% of his baseline PSA.
evidence: This describes the treatment protocol for stopping therapy.

claim: Sixteen patients who were treated with continuous abiraterone as the SOC and met the eligibility criteria for adaptive therapy were identified through chart review.
source: Sixteen patients who were treated with continuous abiraterone as the SOC and met the eligibility criteria for our adaptive therapy were identified through chart review of mCRPC patients treated at the Moffitt Cancer Center during the time of the study enrollment.
evidence: This describes how the control cohort was identified.

claim: All patients in the SOC group had a >50% decline in PSA following initial administration of abiraterone.
source: Thus, all patients fulfilled trial eligibility requirements (including a >50% drop in PSA) and chose SOC treatment. Specifically, all patients in this group had a >50% decline in PSA following initial administration of abiraterone (Appendix 1)
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the control cohort with reference to appendix data.

claim: The original mathematical model divided prostate cancer subpopulations based on their interactions with testosterone: T+ cells require extrinsic androgen, TP cells produce testosterone via upregulated CYP17a1, and T- cells are androgen independent.
source: Our original mathematical model (Zhang et al., 2017) divided the prostate cancer subpopulations based on their interactions with testosterone: T+ cells require extrinsic androgen for survival and proliferation, TP cells require androgen for survival and proliferation but upregulated CYP17a1 (Mostaghel et al., 2011) allow them to produce testosterone generating an autocrine loop, T-cells are androgen independent.
evidence: This describes the mathematical model with citations to prior work.

claim: TP cells producing testosterone represents a 'common good' or 'public good' that can be used by T+ cells.
source: Note the potential coupling of TP and T+ cells as the testosterone produced by the TP cells represent a 'common good' or'public good' (Johnstone and Rodrigues, 2016) that can be used by the T+ cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model dynamics supported by a citation to evolutionary biology literature.

claim: T+ cells act as 'cheaters' because they use the testosterone produced by TP cells but do not incur the fitness cost of producing it.
source: In evolutionary terms, this coupling results in the T+ cells acting as 'cheaters' (Ghoul et al., 2014) because they use the testosterone produced by the TP cells but do not incur the fitness cost of producing it.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model dynamics supported by a citation to evolutionary biology literature.

claim: For post-trial analysis, the T+ and TP cells were combined as both being sensitive to abiraterone.
source: Here, for our post-trial analysis, we combine the T+ and TP cells as both being sensitive to abiraterone.
evidence: This describes a simplification made in the mathematical model for analysis.

claim: Lotka–Volterra competition equations were used to model the interactions between cell types.
source: As in our original report (Zhang et al., 2017), we use Lotka–Volterra (LV) competition equations to model the interactions between the three (prior model) and two (current analysis) cell types
evidence: This describes the mathematical framework used, with citation to prior work.

claim: Since patients are included in the study only if their PSA declined by at least 50% after initial application of abiraterone, the sensitive cells must be more prevalent than the resistant cells.
source: Since patients are included in the study only if their PSA declined by at least 50% after initial application of abiraterone, the sensitive cells must be more prevalent than the resistant cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the trial inclusion criteria and PSA as a marker of tumor burden.

claim: Based on census methodologies and the steep drop in PSA with therapy, the sensitive cells are fitter than the T- cells prior to treatment.
source: Based on census methodologies (Pfister, 1995) and the steep drop in PSA with therapy, we can conclude that the sensitive cells are fitter than the T- cells prior to treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological census methods and observed PSA dynamics, supported by citation.

claim: The assumption that each phenotype produces roughly equal amounts of PSA may introduce error if substantially violated.
source: We assume that each phenotype produces roughly equal amounts of PSA, which may introduce error if this assumption is substantially violated.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a model assumption and its potential limitations.

claim: PSA can be considered a direct estimator of the total number of cancer cells.
source: This assumption does allow us to consider PSA as a direct estimator of the total number of cancer cells.
evidence: This is a model assumption based on the relationship between PSA and tumor burden.

claim: Abiraterone therapy reduces the carrying capacities of the TP and T+ cells, with no effect on T- cells.
source: As in our original model, we let abiraterone therapy reduce the carrying capacities of the TP and T+ cells, with no effect on T-.
evidence: This describes a key assumption in the mathematical model.

claim: TP cells are either killed or quiescent during abiraterone treatment.
source: We assume that TP cells are either killed or quiescent during abiraterone treatment.
evidence: This is a model assumption about the effect of abiraterone.

claim: Since abiraterone inhibits testosterone production by TP cells, the T+ 'cheater' population will have no source of testosterone and decline with abiraterone.
source: Since abiraterone inhibits the production of testosterone by the TP cells, the T+ 'cheater' population will have no source of testosterone and they too decline with abiraterone, rendering both sensitive to abiraterone both directly and indirectly.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of action based on the model structure.

claim: Tumor stage, initial Gleason Scores, and pretreatment PSA values were not significantly different between trial and SOC cohorts.
source: Tumor stage, initial Gleason Scores, and pretreatment PSA values were not significant between both trial and SOC cohorts (Table 1): Gleason scores: Kruskal–Wallis test statistic of 0.088 with p=0.767 based on a chi-square distribution, df = 1. Pretreatment PSA levels: Kruskal–Wallis test statistic of 0.157 with p=0.692 based on a chi-square distribution, df = 1.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of baseline characteristics with test statistics provided, referencing Table 1.

claim: All patients fulfilled trial eligibility so that pretreatment history was identical.
source: All patients fulfilled trial eligibility so that pretreatment history was identical.
evidence: This describes the comparability of the two cohorts.

claim: The study was conducted before abiraterone, enzalutamide, or apalutamide was approved for treating castration-sensitive prostate cancer.
source: This study was conducted before abiraterone was approved in the castration-sensitive setting. None of the patients enrolled in the adaptive therapy trial or included in the historical control had received new hormonal agent (abiraterone, enzalutamide, or apalutamide) or docetaxel in the castration-sensitive setting.
evidence: This provides context about the timing of the study relative to treatment approvals.

claim: Abiraterone was the frontline therapy for mCRPC for most patients in each group.
source: Abiraterone was the frontline therapy for mCRPC for most patients in each group.
evidence: This describes the treatment history of the cohorts.

claim: More patients in the study cohort had >50% PSA reduction within a month due to more frequent PSA checks.
source: Given patients enrolled in the study had more frequent PSA checks than the historical control arm, more patients in the study cohort had >50% PSA reduction within a month.
evidence: This is an observation about differences in monitoring frequency and its effect on measured outcomes.

claim: The percentage of patients who had more than 50% PSA reduction within 2 months was similar: 15/17 (88%) vs. 12/16 (75%).
source: The percentage of patients who had more than 50% PSA reduction within 2 months was similar: 15/17 (88%) vs. 12/16 (75%).
evidence: This is a comparison of response rates between cohorts.

claim: All 16 patients in the SOC group have progressed and all have died at the time of this report.
source: All 16 patients in the SOC group have progressed and all have died at the time of this report.
evidence: This is an observational outcome from the trial follow-up.

claim: Seven patients in the adaptive therapy remain alive at the time of submission.
source: Seven patients in the adaptive therapy remain alive and four patients remain on study without imaging progression (range 53–70 months) as of the date of submission.
evidence: This is an observational outcome from the trial follow-up.

claim: Patients in the adaptive therapy group received an average abiraterone dosing rate of 54% compared to SOC.
source: Patients in the adaptive therapy group received an average abiraterone dosing rate (mg drug/patient/unit time) of 54% compared to SOC.
evidence: This is a calculated metric from the trial data showing reduced drug exposure.

claim: Longitudinal trial data allowed estimation of key model parameters, including growth rate, pretreatment ratio of sensitive and resistant cell populations, and the relative fitness of each population.
source: First, longitudinal trial data allowed key model parameters, including growth rate, pretreatment ratio of sensitive and resistant cell populations, and the relative fitness of each population.
evidence: This describes the mathematical analysis approach using trial data.

claim: ADT was continued during abiraterone therapy.
source: Because ADT was continued during abiraterone therapy, we assumed that the T+ cell proliferation was linked exclusively to androgen production by the TP cells.
evidence: This describes the treatment protocol and a model assumption based on it.

claim: Loss of TP cells would reduce intratumoral androgen concentrations necessitating a decline in the T+ population.
source: That is, loss of TP cells would reduce intratumoral androgen concentrations necessitating a decline in the T+ population.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological mechanism based on the model structure.

claim: The carrying capacity was arbitrarily set to 10,000 as it is scalable.
source: We arbitrarily set the carrying capacity to 10,000 (its scalable).
evidence: This describes a parameter choice in the mathematical model.

claim: All cell types are assumed to have the same carrying capacity.
source: and we assume all cell types have the same carrying capacity.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: Lack of testosterone induces a 90% drop in nutrient and space use efficiency.
source: Thus, we assume that under no therapy all cell types have the same need and utilization of nutrients and space, and we assume lack of testosterone induces a 90% drop in nutrient and space use efficiency.
evidence: This is a model assumption about the effect of abiraterone on carrying capacity.

claim: In the absence of abiraterone, any competitive advantage of the sensitive cells will manifest through either a higher growth rate or a larger competitive effect of sensitive cells on resistant cells than vice versa (αRS > αSR).
source: Finally, in the absence of abiraterone, any competitive advantage of the sensitive cells will manifest through either a higher growth rate, r (only meaningful during transient dynamics away from carrying capacity), or a larger competitive effect of sensitive cells on resistant cells than vice versa (the most salient from a cost of resistance): αRS > αSR.
evidence: This is an inference about how fitness differences manifest in the model parameters.

claim: A two-step process was used for parameter estimation.
source: We used a two-step process for parameter estimation.
evidence: This describes the methodology for parameter estimation.

claim: For each patient, the initial rate of increase of PSA was used to estimate the growth rate of sensitive cells, rS.
source: First, for each patient (dropping those with insufficient pre-therapy data), we used the initial rate of increase of PSA to estimate the growth rate of sensitive cells, rS.
evidence: This describes the methodology for estimating a key parameter from patient data.

claim: The average of patient-specific estimates of rS was used as the patient-wide value for subsequent parameter estimation in both cohorts.
source: We then used the average of these patient-specific estimates of rS as the patient-wide value for subsequent parameter estimation in both the trial and continuous therapy cohorts.
evidence: This describes the methodology for parameter estimation.

claim: Prior to therapy, resistant cells represent a small fraction of extant cancer cells.
source: This assumes that prior to therapy, resistant cells represent a small fraction of extant cancer cells.
evidence: This is a model assumption based on the observed PSA response to therapy.

claim: To estimate the growth rate of resistant cells, the increase in PSA levels following disease progression in the continuous therapy cohort was used under the assumption that with disease progression the cancer cell population is predominately resistant.
source: To estimate the growth rate of resistant cells, we used the increase in PSA levels following disease progression in the continuous therapy cohort under the assumption that with disease progression the cancer cell population is predominately resistant.
evidence: This describes the methodology for estimating a key parameter from patient data.

claim: The competitive effect of resistant cells on sensitive cells was set to αRS = 1, the same as the intraspecific competition coefficients.
source: We set the competitive effect of resistant cells on sensitive cells to αRS = 1, the same as the intraspecific competition coefficients.
evidence: This describes a parameter choice in the mathematical model.

claim: The sensitive cell population had a significantly higher mean growth rate (0.0156 per day) than that for resistant cells (0.0091 per day; p<0.05).
source: The sensitive cell population had a significantly higher mean growth rate (0.0156 per day [population increase of 1.56% per day]) than that for resistant cells (0.0091 per day [increase of 0.91% per day]; p<0.05; Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical analysis of trial data with statistical significance.

claim: Both growth rate values are well within the range observed in clinical cancers.
source: Both values are well within the range observed in clinical cancers (He et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on cancer growth rates.

claim: The difference in growth rates is consistent with the theoretical premise that resistance incurs a cost that decreases fitness and proliferation when therapy is not applied.
source: and the difference is consistent with our theoretical premise that resistance incurs a cost that decreases fitness and proliferation when therapy is not applied.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the observed data to the theoretical framework.

claim: Mathematical estimates of pretreatment fractions of sensitive and resistant cells correlated with subsequent radiographic TTP in both cohorts.
source: Mathematical estimates of pretreatment fractions of sensitive and resistant cells correlated with subsequent radiographic TTP in both cohorts (Figure 2, Figure 3)
evidence: This is a result from the mathematical analysis showing correlation with clinical outcomes, referencing figures.
